In nineteen sixty-nine, Laurence Peter made a joke that stuck: in any hierarchy, people rise to their level of incompetence.
Forty years later, three researchers in Italy built that company inside a computer: a hundred and sixty people, on six floors.
Every year, anyone who is bad at their job is fired, anyone over sixty retires, and each empty desk goes to someone from the floor below.
Common sense says: promote the best. If you're good at your job, you'll be good at the next one.
But the next job is often a different job. A great salesperson can make a terrible sales manager.
So the researchers tried a second rule, Peter's rule: after a promotion, your competence starts over, at random.
Under Peter's rule, promoting the best made the whole company worse. Its efficiency fell by about ten points.
Good workers kept climbing until they landed in a job they were bad at. And there they stayed.
Stranger still, promoting the worst made it better, by about twelve points.
Since nobody knows which rule is true, the safest choice was a coin flip: promote the best or the worst, at random.
Sometimes the rule that feels fairest is also the riskiest one.
